column3: This is VLA Forge. A company describes its line in plain words, and gets a trained robot policy for each station in minutes. All of this runs in simulation.
In the editor you type a task. Here, an SO-101 puts a green block in a slot of the pallet tray, a harder kitting skill.
The agents write the success check, collect demos, fine-tune from the closest skill, then test the policy on {n} scenes it never saw. The waiting is sped up four times, and the badge shows it.
The first round got {r1} of {rn}, under the bar, so the critic sent it back for another.
The new skill trained in {t} seconds and got {s} of {n} held-out scenes, in simulation.
Now the factory line. In Housing Assembly, one SO-101 seats each housing in a pallet slot, a second one inserts it into a socket, and a scripted ViperX crates the result.
Pallet seating got {a0} of {n0} held-out scenes, and {a1} of {a2} on the line. Socket insertion got {b0} of {n1}, and {b1} of {b2}. The scripted crate step got {c1} of {c2}. All in simulation.
End to end, {done} of {parts} parts made it into the crate, at about {tpm} parts a minute of simulated time.
Every skill is saved in the library as a tile with its measured success, including the harder ones: kitting, insertion, and rotate and place.
Ask for something the arm can't reach, like lifting a block sixty centimeters, and the router says not feasible. The jaws top out at fifty-three.
In the Robot tab you build the arm itself. Every part has a preview, and each one is a real open-source model.
That is VLA Forge: describe the line, and get a measured policy for every station, in simulation.
